from: a first week on the desk
to: running a desk and answering to editors, lawyers and foreign bureaux
case_setting: a named part of a newsroom
series_arc: first week on the desk → **running a desk and speaking for the outlet**
learners: They are about to join, or have just joined, a Syrian newspaper, website, agency or broadcaster — where English is the language of the wires, of every foreign bureau and agency, and of the paper trail: contributor agreements, syndication terms, accreditation files, legal notes, correction requests and the messages that arrive from eight countries.
neutral: It is **desk-neutral within journalism**. One cohort can contain a news reporter, a picture editor and a court correspondent, and all three practise the same skill in their own part of the newsroom.
contexts_intro: The programme assumes learners work on different desks, not one. Twelve journalism contexts carry the case studies:
upward: **Upward and outward paper:** shift logs, corrections and incident notes, monthly returns, decision papers for an editor, claims on agencies and contributors, submissions to an accreditation office and replies to complaints — usually written, usually read by somebody who was not there.
contact: **Bureau, agency and source contact:** foreign bureaux and wire agencies, fixers and stringers, press offices, lawyers and contributors, often where neither side is a native speaker.
reading_rows: Profiles, logs, messages, notebook pages — 131–187 words
Incident notes, corrections, options papers, figures explained — 190–290 words
Decision papers, standards, submissions, hearings — 270–356 words
writing_rows: Notes, slips, logs, a three-line handover — 42–66 words
Decision papers, standards, appraisals, submissions — 145–225 words
move3: Decide, supervise, and speak for the outlet
resp2: a story, a source and a figure
resp2b: a story, a source and a figure
arc2: someone who owns a story, a source and a figure
threads: **being honest about what you did not do and cannot evidence** (Course 1 S9 → Course 2 S14 → Course 3 S28); **giving a number its unit, basis and source** (C1 S4 → C2 S16 and S20 → C3 S27); and **writing so that the reader can act** (C1 S12 → C2 S19 → C3 S25).

map_example: A learner on the picture desk meets their own work in sessions 2, 17 and 32, each time at a higher level of responsibility.
posts1: News trainee · reporter on the early or late website shift · wire and copy assistant · picture desk assistant · checker · court or council round reporter · desk clerk taking calls and messages
gives1: Being understood on the desk and in the field, taking a quotation accurately, keeping a log and a register a second person can trust, answering for the outlet on the telephone, holding a consent or legal rule under pressure, accounting for a shift and handing it on
posts2: Reporter with a beat · court or business correspondent · picture editor · verification editor · foreign desk liaison · investigations reporter · duty or night editor
gives2: Owning a story and a source: explaining a correction so a reader who was not there can follow it, training somebody on live copy, explaining why a figure moved, pressing a claim on an agency or a contributor, recommending with a reservation, and being on the record at the morning conference
posts3: News editor · head of the picture desk · investigations editor · foreign editor · managing editor · deputy editor · editor of a website or supplement
gives3: Other people's work and the outlet's word: delegating, appraising, chairing an editorial meeting, writing the standard a desk follows, naming risk before it lands, negotiating with agencies and platforms, disagreeing upward, and answering an accreditation office
constraint: a capable young reporter at the staff grade
sub1: From your first day on the desk to a reporter the desk can send out
sub2: From dependable pair of hands to owning a story, a source and a deadline
sub3: From owning a story to running a desk and answering to editors, lawyers and foreign bureaux
arc1_text: The learner arrives on a desk unable to operate, and leaves able to be relied on: to take a quotation accurately, keep a log and a register a second person can trust, answer for the outlet on the telephone, be trusted with equipment, recordings and accreditation, hold a consent or legal rule under pressure, account for a shift and hand it on.
arc2_text: The learner is given something of their own — a story, a source, a round, a figure — and learns the language that ownership requires: explaining an error so that a reader who was not there can follow it, training somebody on live copy, explaining why a figure moved, pressing a claim on an agency, recommending with a reservation, and reporting upward including what did not happen.
arc3_text: The learner becomes answerable for other people's work and for the outlet's word. Three sessions are given to supervision itself — delegating, appraising and chairing — and the course runs on through writing the standard a desk follows, naming risk before it lands, negotiating with agencies and contributors, answering an accreditation office, and arguing for the learner's own next post.
